content:
Ghost stories give old haunts new life

In the heart of Port Townsend, there are shadows haunting visible and invisible corners. According to local historian Joyce Hester, the heart of the town is full of history surrounding nearly every building.

Historian Joyce Hester is a tour guide for Haunted Histories and Mysteries downtown walking tour. Above, the Manresa Castle. Photo courtesy of Joyce Hester

“Pick a building, and chances are there’s a ghost story,” Hester said. “Hotels seem to have many stories, but maybe that’s because of the massive amount of people coming through.”

Clockwise from top left: Adele and Israel Katz pose for a photographer sometime after their marriage in 1894. Mr. Katz disappeared around 1914-15, when he was about 64 years old. Photo courtesy of JCHS and Kelsey Caudebec

Hester noted that the Hastings Building, whose top floors have been vacant for decades, has drawn paranormal activity, including experiences reported by children.

Normally closed to the public, the historic jail’s exercise yard is unlocked at the end of the ‘Strange Shadows’ walking tour, when guides lead visitors into the jail spaces for an exclusive interpretive experience. Photo courtesy of JCHS/Kelsey Caudebec

Hester said the stories she recounts on her walking tours are always authentic.

“Some are firsthand accounts presented to our staff, or lived by our staff,” Hester said. “Some have been researched professionally by ghost hunters whom we’ve employed.”

Manresa Castle stands overlooking the City of Port Townsend and Port Townsend Bay. Built in 1892 as a grand Victorian home by first mayor Charles Eisenbeis, it was later used as a Jesuit training college and now operates as a historic hotel. It is widely known for its ghost stories and active paranormal reputation.  Photos courtesy of the Jefferson County Historical Society

Hester has served as one of the volunteer walking guides for Port Townsend Main Street’s “Haunted Histories and Mysteries” walking tours.

The Captain Tibbals Building, circa 1903, at the intersection of Water and Tyler Streets is home to the Palace Hotel. The hotel is listed as one of Port Townsend’s haunted hot spots with some sources claiming the site houses as many as 10 spirits. Photo courtesy of the Jefferson County Historical Society

Port Townsend’s darker past also supports its haunted legends.

“Forced men in the thousands were pressed into duty on ships,” Hester said. “The sex trade was booming. Opium houses were fashionable.”

The Hastings Building stands tall on Water Street. With its upper floors vacant for many decades, the historic building has had numerous spirits documented by professional paranormal investigators. Leader photo by Jon Decker

While buildings of the original tenderloin district have been lost for decades, Hester asserted that tales are still hidden in the town’s collective consciousness, just waiting to be uncovered by those brave enough to walk down its fog-shrouded streets.

The restored Victorian architecture of the town adds to the feeling of entering a different time.

“Being in Port Townsend is like going back in time, to an era when the occult and the spiritual were a major part of the culture,” Hester said. “The atmosphere certainly invites the imagination.”

Hester believes this lends a timelessness to Port Townsend’s stories.

“I also think that the stories are timeless because they recycle all the time,” Hester said. “Every time I get an annual update at a hotel, they always have a fresh set of encounters to share.”

For those who return to Port Townsend each October, the past is never really left behind, as Hester promises that it lingers in every alley and corridor, in the dark corners.

VICTORIAN SEAPORT HISTORIC LANDMARK

“As for the Victorian architecture itself — I do think, if you use your imagination a little bit, you could say that it can lend itself a little bit of spookiness around Halloween, if you’re willing to see it that way — the fact that we’re so well-preserved is tied very directly to the boom and bust of the early 1890s,” said Kelsey Caudebec, Jefferson County Historical Society program manager. The society also runs Halloween-season walking tours of their own.

Caudebec said that, while most older towns have boom-and-bust histories, Port Townsend’s is “really dramatic in terms of how large the boom was, and then how large the letdown.”

When the railroad did not come, and the panic of 1893 hit, “Much of downtown and uptown were really ‘frozen in time,’ so to speak,” Caudebec said.

Port Townsend is one of three Victorian Seaport Historic Landmark districts in the country, but in Caudebec’s estimation, it rises to the top, “due to how incredibly well-preserved we are.”

“The haunted history tours attract people to visit Port Townsend during the fall, since it’s a special attraction that is unique to Port Townsend history,” said Natalie Maitland, executive director of the Port Townsend Main Street Program.

Maitland said interest has expanded to include Fort Worden, among numerous other hot spots in October.

“There’s lore and fact-based ghost stories, which is a nice mix of allowing people to place their own twist on some of the stories that are being shared,” Maitland said.

Hester, who’s served as one of the volunteer walking guides for Main Street’s “Haunted Histories and Mysteries,” described a town filled with ghosts.

Hester said, “Ghost-seekers years ago recorded a variety of occurrences within the Hastings building, including some involving children.”

According to Hester, these stories are researched thoroughly.

“Some are firsthand accounts related to our team, or suffered by our team,” Hester said. “Some are supported by historical records, such as newspaper articles, memoirs or court papers. And some have been investigated by professional paranormal researchers that we have consulted.”

Hester said Port Townsend’s darker history carries a ghostly reputation.

“None of the stories that we share are considered to be fabricated,” Hester said.

“STRANGE SHADOWS”

The Jefferson County Historical Society museum lobby and one of the historic jail cells are decked out from Tuesday, Oct. 27, through Sunday, Nov. 1, and its resident walking tour, “Strange Shadows: Uncanny Tales of Port Townsend,” leads people on a tour of stories of sea monsters, flying saucers, notorious crimpers and some of the town’s most unsettling stories.

“Initially, the plan was for the walking tour to be our regular ‘Legends and Lore of Port Townsend’ tour, but then I spent so much time researching new information and having such a good time doing it that it became something in itself,” Caudebec said.

The tour concludes in the historic jail sections, like the rarely opened exercise yard.

“Many people have been to our jail — it’s part of the museum — but we go a bit deeper into the history of the region,” Caudebec said.

“HAUNTED HISTORIES & MYSTERIES”

Haunted Histories & Mysteries of Port Townsend invites locals and visitors to step into the shadows and explore the town’s legendary past. These guided Haunted Walks weave together true history, local lore and a few lingering mysteries — bringing Port Townsend’s stories to life after dark.
